e.t: This word means “unceasingly”: something is done continually, without coming to an end or being interrupted. It functions as an adverb, describing how an action or practice takes place rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including passages in Romans and 1 Thessalonians. Its central idea is persistent continuation, emphasizing that the action keeps occurring instead of happening only once or occasionally.

This word describes something “never stopping” or “unceasing.” It points to continued activity or persistence rather than something occasional or brief. As a descriptive word, it presents the action or condition as ongoing without interruption. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:14; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains steady continuation: something that does not pause, cease, or let up.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to receive,” describing an act in which something is received. It functions as an action word, focusing on receiving rather than naming a person, place, or thing. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Acts 28:7 and once in Hebrews 11:17. The references identify its locations, while the surrounding verse text is needed to state what was received in each passage.

e.t: This word means “to rebuild”: to build something again after it has been broken down, fallen into ruin, or been removed. It is a verb describing an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within Acts 15:16, so its normal sense is narrowly represented in this corpus. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the restoration or reconstruction of what was previously standing.

me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to take away.” It describes an action in which something or someone is removed from its present place or situation. Because it is a verb, it expresses what happens rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This word means “to store up” or “to store up treasure.” It describes the action of deliberately gathering and keeping something valuable for future use. As a verb, it focuses on building up a reserve rather than receiving or using something immediately. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:19, so its precise force there is understood from that passage’s surrounding words and context.

“Aristobulus” is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Romans 16:10. The name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or circumstances; those details must come from the surrounding passage, which is not included here. Its possessive rendering in one English translation reflects how the name functions in the sentence, not a different meaning.

This word means “on one’s own initiative” or “self-chosen.” It describes something undertaken by personal choice, willingly and without another person directing the decision. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Corinthians 8. Its basic emphasis is that the action comes from the person’s own determination rather than being imposed from outside. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain the specific action being described.

This word refers to an eyewitness—someone who personally saw what happened and can testify about it. It describes direct, firsthand knowledge rather than information received from another person. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 1:2. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a person who witnessed events personally.

e.t: This word means “to delay”: it describes putting something off or allowing it to happen later rather than immediately. It is an action word, focusing on the postponement itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Timothy 3:15 and 2 Peter 3:9. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the act of delaying or holding something back for a time.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to beat up,” describing forceful physical striking or assault. It is used when people are subjected to bodily violence, whether by individuals or authorities. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek New Testament, showing a recurring description of physical mistreatment rather than a general expression for disagreement or hardship. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and who is performing the action.

This word means “justice” or “righteous judgment.” It points to judgment that is right, fair, and consistent with what is righteous. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 2:5, so its normal lexical meaning is clear even though the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word describes justice as a right standard of judgment rather than merely a human opinion about what seems fair.

e.t: This word means “to embrace” or “to take in one’s arms.” It describes the physical action of drawing someone close and holding them with the arms. The meaning is personal and active, referring to an embrace rather than merely being near someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Mark, so it has a focused but clear use within that corpus.

This word means to contend: to make an active effort in support of something rather than remain passive. It describes purposeful engagement in a matter, with the sense of standing firmly for what is being upheld. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: to contend actively and earnestly.

This word means “care” or “needs,” referring to attentive concern given to what someone requires. It presents care as practical attention rather than merely a feeling: taking notice of needs and responding to them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:3. That single occurrence establishes its normal lexical sense, while the surrounding verse and passage determine the specific force of the word there.

e.t: This word means “to make ready” or “to prepare.” It describes arranging, setting up, or getting something or someone ready for what is to come. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 40 times, showing a recurring action rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its use can concern practical preparations as well as readiness for an appointed purpose. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being prepared, but the central sense remains making ready in advance.

This word is the personal name “Zerubbabel,” referring to a specific man rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, all in genealogical passages: twice in Matthew and once in Luke. Because it functions as a person’s name, its meaning is primarily identification. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what is being said about Zerubbabel in any particular occurrence.

This word means “throne”: a royal seat or place of rule. In the Greek New Testament, it names the seat itself rather than an action or quality. It occurs 62 times in 51 verses, making it a recurring term, especially in Revelation, where it appears 47 times. Its range extends from Matthew through Revelation, and the same basic meaning remains whether the word is singular or plural. The precise significance of a particular throne depends on its surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek New Testament word describes cheerfulness—the glad, willing spirit with which a person acts. It points to an attitude of joyful readiness rather than reluctant or gloomy action. “Cheerfully” describes how something is done, while “cheerfulness” names the quality itself. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 12:8. The surrounding verse determines its precise application, but the central idea is a positive, willing disposition expressed in action.

This Greek New Testament word means “step,” “track,” or “tracks,” referring to the marks or path made by someone’s feet. It is a noun used for the physical idea of footsteps and can also describe the path a person follows. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament: once each in Romans, 2 Corinthians, and 1 Peter. Its central picture is movement marked by footsteps, making it suitable for speaking about following someone’s example or walking along a path when the surrounding sentence gives that force.

e.t: This word means “to lord it over” or “to master”—to exercise controlling authority over other people. It describes domination rather than simple service or cooperation, focusing on one person ruling over others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is exercising power over others in a commanding or domineering way.

This word means “throat,” referring to the passage at the front of the neck through which air, food, and speech pass. It is a concrete noun rather than a description of a person’s character or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 3:13. There, its precise force belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself retains its ordinary bodily meaning: the throat as part of the human body.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to serve” or “to minister,” describing devoted service carried out for someone, especially in relation to God. Its glosses also express the idea of being engaged in service rather than merely performing a single task. It occurs 21 times in the Greek New Testament, so it has a broad use across passages about worshipful service and service to God. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to destroy” or “to ravage.” It describes severe damage or ruin brought upon something or someone, rather than a mild disturbance or ordinary harm. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 8:3. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the sentence and wider account. Its basic sense remains an active, forceful destruction that leaves what is attacked seriously damaged.

Macedonia is the name of a place or region. In the New Testament, the word identifies Macedonia as a geographical setting connected with events and movements recorded in the early church. It occurs 22 times across 20 verses, especially in Acts and Paul’s letters. The word itself names the place; the surrounding passage determines what happened there or why it is mentioned. This term appears in Acts, 1 and 2 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians, and 1 Timothy.

Mesopotamia is the name of a region. The word functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts. It is rendered “Mesopotamia” and refers to the geographic region associated with the biblical account. The word appears in Acts 2:9 and Acts 7:2, but understanding its particular significance in either passage requires the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word means “and not” or “neither.” It functions as a negative linking expression, adding another person, thing, or action to what is being denied or excluded. Depending on the sentence, it can connect two negative statements or emphasize that a second possibility is also ruled out. It occurs 34 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is consistent across several kinds of passages.

Nicanor is a personal name, referring to a specific man rather than describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears once, in Acts 6:5. The passage identifies Nicanor among the seven men chosen by the believers in Jerusalem to serve the community. Since this word functions as a name, its meaning is chiefly identifying: it tells the reader who the person is. The name itself does not provide a broader spiritual or moral definition apart from the context in which its bearer is mentioned.

This word means “this.” It is used to point out or identify a particular person, thing, or matter, directing attention to something definite rather than speaking generally. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, so it is an occasional demonstrative word rather than a frequent term. Its exact reference—what “this” points to—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek word describes something as sharp or swift. It can point to a keen edge or blade, and it can also express quickness or speed. In the New Testament, it occurs eight times, with most occurrences in Revelation and one in Romans. Its precise emphasis—sharpness or swiftness—depends on how it functions in the surrounding sentence, but the central idea is something keen, fast, or able to move swiftly.

This word means “region,” referring to a particular geographic area or locality. It identifies a defined part of a larger land or territory rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times across 11 verses, especially in Matthew and Mark. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding passage, but its normal sense is a region or territorial area.

This word means the sense of smell—the ability by which a person or creature detects odors. It refers to one of the bodily senses, alongside seeing, hearing, tasting, and touching. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 12:17. The word itself identifies the faculty of smelling; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

Paphos is a proper place-name, referring to Paphos rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 13. The English Bible renders it consistently as “Paphos,” preserving the name rather than translating it into a descriptive term. Its two recorded occurrences are Acts 13:6 and Acts 13:13; the surrounding verse context would be needed to explain its particular role in either passage.

This Greek New Testament word refers to garbage or scum—something regarded as worthless, filthy, or fit to be cast away. It appears only once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 4:13. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the sentence and paragraph around it. Its basic sense is a deeply low description of something treated as refuse.

This word means “to swell” or “to swell up.” It describes becoming enlarged or distended, and it functions as an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the central idea remains physical swelling or becoming swollen. The word therefore points to a visible increase in size or fullness, expressed as something that swells up.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “about” or “somewhere,” expressing an approximate place or location rather than identifying a precise one. It can also convey the general idea of being in or around a place. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once each in Acts and Romans and twice in Hebrews. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains an intentionally indefinite location.

e.t: This word means “before”. It marks something that happens earlier than another event, statement, or time. It helps arrange people, actions, or moments in sequence, showing what comes first. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 13 times, consistently expressing this idea of prior time. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what follows and the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains clear: one thing occurs or is considered before another.

e.t: This word means “be formerly” or “to exist formerly,” pointing to something that was already present or had existed earlier. It describes prior existence rather than simply naming something as present now. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, so its basic sense is narrowly defined by those two uses. The surrounding verse determines what person or thing is being described, but the word itself directs attention to an earlier state or prior existence.

e.t: This word means “be first” or “to be supreme.” It describes a person who holds the foremost place, standing above others in rank or importance. Its meaning points to priority and recognized supremacy rather than merely being first in time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 1:18. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how this meaning operates there, but the word itself identifies the one who occupies the highest position or has first place.

This word means “with a roar,” describing a loud, rushing sound or the manner in which something happens. It functions as an adverb, adding sound and force to an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 3:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: an action accompanied by a powerful, audible roar.

This word describes someone or something regarded as august and revered—held in especially high honor and treated with deep respect. It expresses dignity that calls for reverence rather than ordinary regard. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts, so its normal sense is connected with a person or designation viewed as highly honored. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “fattened”: made fat or well-fed, usually by being given enough food. It describes an animal prepared to be especially suitable for eating, rather than merely an animal that is alive or available. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Luke 15, where it identifies the fattened animal selected for a celebratory meal. Its central idea is an animal deliberately nourished and prepared for that purpose.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to wrap,” describing something enclosed or covered by wrapping. It is used twice, both in Luke chapter 2, and its wording points to the act or result of wrapping rather than to a person, place, or abstract idea. The central meaning remains simple: something has been wrapped around another thing. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being described.

Shechem is a proper name used as a specific designation rather than a general description. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, with both instances appearing in Acts 7:16, and it is rendered “Shechem.” Its lexical meaning is simply the name itself; its precise referent and significance in that verse are best understood from the surrounding passage. This word is therefore a name, not a general quality or action.

This word means “appointed,” referring to something fixed, designated, or set in place. It describes an arrangement established for a particular purpose or time rather than something accidental or spontaneous. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 12:21, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word therefore emphasizes being assigned or established according to a prior designation. It does not by itself explain who made the appointment or why; those details must come from the context.

e.t: It means to draw back or withdraw—to step away rather than continue openly. The word can describe a person holding back, retreating, or shrinking from something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, so its basic sense is consistent, while its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It appears in Acts, Galatians, and Hebrews, including the idea of drawing back instead of moving forward.

This word describes what is good, kind, or easy. It can express a quality that benefits others, a gracious character, or something that is not difficult to bear. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, showing a focused but varied use: it may describe goodness, kindness, or ease depending on the sentence. Its central idea is positive quality—what is favorable, gentle, or beneficial rather than harsh or harmful.
